experiences.title: Pentecost: wind, fire and tongues in Jerusalem
experiences.account: Acts 2:1-4 (KJV, public domain): "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Luke adds that pilgrims from many nations heard the disciples speaking in their own languages, that some mocked them as drunk, and that Peter explained the event as the fulfilment of Joel 2:28-32. About three thousand are said to have been baptised that day (Acts 2:41).
experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Luke presents the event as the promised outpouring of the Spirit (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8), the reversal of Babel and the birth of the Jerusalem church's mission. Peter's sermon reads it through Joel's prophecy of the 'last days'. Bystanders offered a naturalistic reading (drunkenness), which Peter rejects as it was only the third hour of the day.

assessments.text: Pentecost is the birthday of the Church and the inauguration of its sacramental life; the gift of the Spirit continues in baptism and chrismation/confirmation. Speaking in tongues is accepted as a real apostolic sign, though not regarded as the normative evidence of receiving the Spirit.

Acts 2 is a pattern, not only a one-off: a 'baptism in the Holy Spirit' distinct from conversion, often accompanied by tongues, is available to believers today. Classical Pentecostals (e.g. Assemblies of God) teach tongues as the 'initial physical evidence'.

Pentecost is a unique, unrepeatable redemptive-historical event marking the transition of the covenant; the tongues were real foreign languages that authenticated the apostolic message and ceased with the apostolic era.

Most critical scholars accept that the early Jesus movement experienced ecstatic phenomena (Paul's letters confirm glossolalia at Corinth), but see Luke's narrative, written perhaps 50 years later, as theologically shaped: the list of nations and the xenolalia motif serve his universal-mission theme.

debates: Were the 'tongues' known foreign languages (xenolalia), ecstatic speech (glossolalia), or a miracle of hearing?
Is Spirit baptism subsequent to conversion (Pentecostal) or identical with it (most Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox readings)?
Cessationism vs continuationism: is Acts 2 descriptive history or a normative pattern?
experiences.story:
The setting is Jerusalem a few weeks after the crucifixion of Jesus, around the year 30. Pentecost (Greek for "fiftieth") was the Jewish Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, celebrated fifty days after Passover as a harvest festival and, in some later Jewish tradition, as a commemoration of the giving of the Law at Sinai. It was one of the three pilgrimage feasts, so the city was crowded with Jews and proselytes from across the Diaspora. According to the Acts of the Apostles, the followers of Jesus, about a hundred and twenty people including the eleven apostles, Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers, had been meeting in an upper room, praying and waiting, because the risen Jesus had told them to stay in the city until they were "endued with power from on high" (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:4-8). They had already chosen Matthias to replace Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:15-26).

Luke, the author of Acts, describes what happened on the morning of the feast. A sound "as of a rushing mighty wind" filled the house, something like divided tongues of fire rested on each of them, and they "began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance" (Acts 2:2-4, KJV). The noise drew a crowd. Luke lists the visitors by origin, from Parthians, Medes and Elamites in the east to Cretans, Arabians and visitors from Rome in the west, and reports that each heard the disciples speaking in his own language about "the wonderful works of God". Some were amazed; others mocked, saying the speakers were "full of new wine".

Peter, the fisherman from Galilee who only weeks earlier had denied knowing Jesus, then stood up with the eleven and addressed the crowd. According to Acts 2:14-36 he rejected the charge of drunkenness, since it was only the third hour of the day (about nine in the morning), and explained the event through the prophecy of Joel 2:28-32: in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on all flesh, so that sons and daughters would prophesy, young men see visions and old men dream dreams. He went on to proclaim that Jesus, whom the authorities had crucified, had been raised by God and exalted, and that it was he who had poured out what they now saw and heard.

Luke reports that the listeners were "pricked in their heart" and asked what they should do. Peter told them to repent and be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, promising that they would receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, a promise "unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off" (Acts 2:38-39). About three thousand people are said to have been baptised that day. The chapter closes with a portrait of the new community: devoted to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayers, sharing goods, meeting daily in the Temple and in homes (Acts 2:42-47).

The only narrative source is Acts, written probably some decades later (most scholars date it between about 70 and 100, a minority earlier). Historians therefore read it carefully. Many accept a core memory of an early, collective experience of ecstatic speech and Spirit-possession among Jesus' followers in Jerusalem, since Paul independently attests tongues, prophecy and a sense of the Spirit's presence in his churches in the 50s (1 Corinthians 12-14). Others think Luke has shaped the scene theologically: the list of nations recalls the table of nations in Genesis 10 and reverses the confusion of languages at Babel, and the wind and fire echo Sinai. There is also a long debate about whether Luke means real foreign languages (xenolalia), an unintelligible speech heard as language (a 'miracle of hearing'), or something closer to the glossolalia Paul describes.

Whatever its exact form, the event became the founding story of the church's mission. Acts structures its whole narrative from it, as the gospel moves from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and "the uttermost part of the earth" (Acts 1:8). The feast of Pentecost was being kept by Christians by the second century, and by the fourth it was a major baptismal season. In East and West it is celebrated as the descent of the Holy Spirit and often called the birthday of the Church.

In the twentieth century the story took on new life. Charles Parham's students in Topeka (1901) and the Azusa Street mission in Los Angeles (1906) understood their own experiences of tongues as a restoration of Acts 2, and the movement they began took its name from it: Pentecostalism. For hundreds of millions of Christians today, this chapter is not only history but a pattern they expect to see repeated.

keyMoments.text: Jesus' followers, about a hundred and twenty people, gather in Jerusalem to pray after his ascension, as Luke reports in Acts 1.
On the Feast of Weeks a sound like wind and tongues like fire come upon the gathered disciples, and they begin to speak in other tongues (Acts 2:1-4).
Pilgrims from across the Diaspora hear the disciples in their own languages; some are amazed and others mock them as drunk.
Peter preaches that the event fulfils Joel's prophecy and proclaims the crucified Jesus as risen Lord and Messiah.
About three thousand are said to be baptised, and a community of shared teaching, meals, prayer and goods forms (Acts 2:41-47).
Paul's letters from the 50s attest tongues and prophecy in his churches, independent evidence of early charismatic experience (1 Corinthians 12-14).
The Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles interprets its experiences as a renewed Pentecost, and the global Pentecostal movement takes its name from Acts 2.

experiences.significance: Pentecost is the founding narrative of the Christian church's identity and mission: it gives the Holy Spirit a central place in Christian experience and frames the gospel as meant for every language and nation. Catholic and Orthodox traditions read it as the birth of the Church and connect it to baptism and chrismation or confirmation; Protestant traditions stress the preaching of the Word and conversion; Pentecostal and charismatic movements, now a quarter or more of world Christianity by some estimates, treat it as a repeatable pattern of Spirit baptism with tongues. Critical scholars debate how much of Luke's account is reportage and how much theological shaping, and what exactly 'other tongues' meant, but most accept that early Christianity was marked by intense collective experiences of the Spirit.

experiences.title: Paul's encounter on the Damascus road
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Acts 9:1-19 (also told in Acts 22 and 26): travelling to Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus, Saul is surrounded by a light from heaven, falls to the ground and hears a voice asking why he persecutes him; the voice identifies itself as Jesus. Saul is left blind for three days until Ananias lays hands on him, 'something like scales' fall from his eyes and he is baptised. In his own letters Paul says only that God 'revealed his Son' in him (Galatians 1:15-16) and that the risen Christ 'appeared' to him last of all (1 Corinthians 15:8).

primarySource.title: Acts of the Apostles 9, 22, 26; Paul's letters

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: For Luke and Paul this was a resurrection appearance and a prophetic call to the Gentiles, not merely an inward change of mind. Paul treats it as the basis of his apostolic authority. In 2 Corinthians 12 he separately describes being 'caught up to the third heaven', which later mystics took as a model of rapture.

assessments.text: A genuine appearance of the risen Christ and the paradigm of conversion and vocation; the Feast of the Conversion of St Paul (25 January) has been kept in the West since the early Middle Ages.
A model for direct encounter with Christ, healing through the laying on of hands and being 'filled with the Holy Spirit' (Acts 9:17).

Paul's own testimony is first-hand and early (c. AD 50s), making this one of the best-attested religious experiences of antiquity; the three Acts versions differ in detail (who heard the voice, who saw the light), which scholars treat as Luke's literary variation.

Since William James the episode has been a classic case of sudden conversion; proposed explanations (guilt-driven crisis, temporal-lobe phenomena) are speculative and cannot be tested on a two-thousand-year-old report.

debates: Was Paul's experience 'objective' (seen by companions) or visionary? The Acts accounts differ.
Is Paul's conversion a 'conversion' at all, or a prophetic call within Judaism (Krister Stendahl's question)?
experiences.story:
Saul of Tarsus was a Greek-speaking Jew from Cilicia, a Roman citizen according to Acts, trained as a Pharisee and, by his own account, "exceedingly zealous" for the traditions of his ancestors (Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:5-6). In the first years after Jesus' death the new movement of his followers was spreading among Jews in Jerusalem and beyond. Saul regarded it as a dangerous deviation. Acts places him at the stoning of Stephen, guarding the clothes of the executioners (Acts 7:58-8:1), and describes him going from house to house to drag believers to prison. Paul himself later admitted that he had "persecuted the church of God" and tried to destroy it (Galatians 1:13; 1 Corinthians 15:9).

According to Acts 9, Saul obtained letters from the high priest authorising him to arrest followers of "the Way" in the synagogues of Damascus and bring them bound to Jerusalem. The date is usually placed within a few years of the crucifixion, around 33-36. As he approached the city, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" When he asked who was speaking, the answer came, "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest" (Acts 9:4-5, KJV). He was told to go into the city and wait for instructions.

His companions, according to Acts 9, heard the voice but saw no one; in the retelling of Acts 22 they saw the light but did not hear the voice. Saul got up blind and had to be led by the hand into Damascus, where he stayed three days without eating or drinking. Then a disciple in the city named Ananias, after objecting in a vision that this man was known for harming believers, was told that Saul was a "chosen vessel" to carry Jesus' name to Gentiles, kings and Israel. Ananias went to the house of Judas on the street called Straight, laid hands on him, and "there fell from his eyes as it had been scales". Saul was baptised and soon began preaching in the synagogues that Jesus was the Son of God, to the astonishment of those who knew why he had come.

Acts tells the story three times, once in narrative (chapter 9) and twice in Paul's own speeches, before a Jerusalem crowd (chapter 22) and before King Agrippa II (chapter 26), and the details vary slightly, which historians usually take as a sign of oral retelling rather than invention. Paul's own letters never narrate the scene, but they refer to it as an event in which the risen Christ "was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time" (1 Corinthians 15:8) and in which God "revealed his Son in me, that I might preach him among the heathen" (Galatians 1:15-16). He treated it as the basis of his apostleship.

The aftermath was complicated. Paul says that he went away into "Arabia" (probably the Nabataean kingdom) and returned to Damascus, and only after three years went up to Jerusalem to meet Cephas (Peter) for fifteen days (Galatians 1:17-18). Both Paul and Acts record a dramatic escape from Damascus, lowered in a basket through an opening in the city wall to evade arrest; Paul names the ethnarch of King Aretas as the one guarding the city (2 Corinthians 11:32-33; Acts 9:23-25). Believers in Jerusalem were at first afraid of him until Barnabas vouched for him (Acts 9:26-27).

From this turning point came the missionary career that carried the gospel through Syria, Asia Minor, Macedonia and Greece, and the letters that form nearly half of the New Testament books. Paul's insistence that Gentile converts need not be circumcised or keep the whole Mosaic Law, which he connected with the grace he himself had received, was debated at the meeting in Jerusalem around 49 and in his letter to the Galatians.

The phrase "Damascus road" passed into ordinary speech for any sudden, life-changing reversal. Historians and theologians have argued about what to call it. Traditional readings, especially since Augustine and Luther, see a conversion from guilt to grace. In 1963 Krister Stendahl argued that Paul experienced a prophetic call, like Jeremiah's, rather than a conversion from one religion to another, since he remained a Jew; later 'New Perspective' scholars developed related readings. Psychological and medical explanations, from visionary experience to epilepsy, have also been proposed, though the evidence for any diagnosis is thin.

keyMoments.text: Saul, a zealous Pharisee, takes part in suppressing the Jesus movement, and Acts places him at the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7:58-8:3).
Carrying letters from the high priest, Saul travels toward Damascus to arrest followers of 'the Way' (Acts 9:1-2).
Near Damascus a light from heaven flashes around him and a voice identifies itself as Jesus whom he is persecuting (Acts 9:3-6).
Blinded, Saul is led into the city and fasts for three days before Ananias lays hands on him, his sight returns, and he is baptised (Acts 9:8-18).
Saul begins preaching Jesus in the synagogues of Damascus and then goes away into 'Arabia' (Galatians 1:17).
After escaping Damascus in a basket let down through the wall, Paul visits Peter in Jerusalem for fifteen days (2 Corinthians 11:32-33; Galatians 1:18).
Paul defends his law-free gospel for Gentiles at the meeting with the Jerusalem leaders (Galatians 2; Acts 15).

experiences.significance: Paul's experience near Damascus made a persecutor into the most influential early missionary and author of Christianity, and his Gentile mission shaped the movement into a largely non-Jewish, transnational faith. His interpretation of the event as unearned grace became central to Western theology through Augustine and the Reformation, while the Eastern churches emphasise it as illumination and apostolic calling. Modern scholarship debates whether 'conversion' or 'call' best fits Paul's own understanding, a debate tied to larger arguments about Paul and Judaism. The story also became the archetype of the sudden conversion narrative that later evangelical and revival movements prized.

experiences.title: The Spirit falls on Cornelius' household at Caesarea
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Acts 10-11: the Roman centurion Cornelius sees an angel in a vision telling him to send for Peter; at Joppa Peter has a trance-vision of a sheet of clean and unclean animals and hears 'what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common'. While Peter is preaching in Cornelius' house the Holy Spirit 'fell on all them which heard the word' and they speak with tongues; Peter then has them baptised. In Acts 19:1-7 a similar sequence occurs at Ephesus, where Paul lays hands on about twelve disciples who speak with tongues and prophesy.
experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: In Acts the event settles a controversy: the visible gift of the Spirit to uncircumcised Gentiles convinces the Jerusalem church that Gentiles may be baptised without first becoming Jews, and is cited again at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15:8).

assessments.text: One of the key 'Pentecostal' texts: tongues accompany the coming of the Spirit here as at Pentecost and Ephesus, supporting the doctrine of tongues as initial evidence.
Tongues served here as a one-time public sign that Gentiles were included in the people of God; the episode is descriptive and transitional, not a template for later believers.
The sequence of Spirit, baptism and (at Ephesus) laying on of hands is read in light of baptism and confirmation; the visions show God guiding the Church's apostolic leaders.
Luke uses the episode to legitimate the Gentile mission, a real and divisive issue in the 40s-50s also visible in Galatians 2; the details are shaped by his narrative purpose.

debates: Does the order of events (Spirit before baptism) undermine any fixed sacramental sequence?
Are the Acts tongues-episodes normative or transitional?
experiences.story:
Caesarea Maritima, on the Mediterranean coast of Judea, was the Roman administrative capital of the province, a city built by Herod the Great with a great artificial harbour, a temple to Augustus and a largely non-Jewish population. In the early years of the Jesus movement, perhaps around 40, its members were almost all Jews, together with some Samaritans and at least one Ethiopian official (Acts 8). Whether and how Gentiles could join without first becoming Jews was an open and explosive question.

Acts 10 introduces Cornelius, a centurion of the "Italian band" (cohort), described as a devout man who "feared God with all his house", gave generously to the Jewish people and prayed regularly. He was what Luke and some inscriptions call a God-fearer: a Gentile attracted to Jewish worship without becoming a full proselyte. According to the narrative, at about the ninth hour (three in the afternoon, a Jewish hour of prayer) he saw an angel in a vision, who told him that his prayers and alms had been remembered and that he should send to Joppa for a man named Simon Peter, lodging with Simon the tanner by the sea. Cornelius sent two servants and a devout soldier.

The next day, as the messengers approached Joppa, Peter went up on the flat roof of the house to pray at about noon. He was hungry and, Luke says, fell into a trance. He saw something like a great sheet let down from heaven, containing all kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles and birds, and heard a voice telling him, "Rise, Peter; kill, and eat." Peter refused, saying he had never eaten anything common or unclean, and the voice replied, "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common" (Acts 10:13-15, KJV). This happened three times. While Peter was still puzzling over it, the men from Caesarea arrived, and the Spirit told him to go with them without hesitation.

Peter travelled to Caesarea with several believers from Joppa. Cornelius had gathered his relatives and close friends and, when Peter entered, fell at his feet; Peter raised him, saying that he too was only a man. Peter acknowledged that it was not lawful by custom for a Jew to associate with or visit a foreigner, but said that God had shown him not to call any person common or unclean. After hearing Cornelius' story, he began to speak: "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: but in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him" (Acts 10:34-35). He summarised the ministry, death and resurrection of Jesus.

While Peter was still speaking, Luke reports, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. The Jewish believers who had come with Peter were astonished, "because that on the Gentiles also was poured out the gift of the Holy Ghost. For they heard them speak with tongues, and magnify God" (Acts 10:45-46). Peter asked whether anyone could refuse water for baptism to those who had received the Spirit just as the apostles had, and he ordered them to be baptised in the name of the Lord. He stayed with them for some days, sharing their hospitality.

The reaction in Jerusalem was not welcoming. According to Acts 11, the circumcision party criticised Peter for going into the house of uncircumcised men and eating with them. Peter retold the whole story step by step, ending with the coming of the Spirit, and asked, "what was I, that I could withstand God?" His critics fell silent and glorified God for granting Gentiles repentance unto life. The question was not settled for good: the controversy at Antioch over table fellowship (Galatians 2:11-14) and the meeting of apostles and elders in Jerusalem around 49, where Peter is said to have cited this episode (Acts 15:7-11), show that it remained contested.

Historians note that Luke gives this story unusual weight, telling it twice in full and referring to it a third time, which signals that he regarded it as a turning point. Some scholars think Luke has idealised a more gradual and conflicted process in which Gentile mission began in places like Antioch (Acts 11:20); others see a genuine early memory of a Gentile household receiving the Spirit that helped justify the Gentile mission.

keyMoments.text: Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea, sees an angel at the ninth hour and is told to send for Peter (Acts 10:1-8).
Peter, praying on a rooftop in Joppa, sees a sheet full of clean and unclean animals and hears that what God has cleansed is not to be called common (Acts 10:9-16).
Cornelius' messengers arrive, and Peter goes with them to Caesarea with believers from Joppa (Acts 10:17-24).
Peter preaches to Cornelius' household that God shows no partiality among nations (Acts 10:34-43).
The Spirit falls on the Gentile listeners, who speak in tongues, and Peter has them baptised (Acts 10:44-48).
Peter defends his action before critics in Jerusalem, who accept that God has granted repentance to the Gentiles (Acts 11:1-18).
At the Jerusalem meeting Peter cites the Cornelius episode in the debate over circumcision of Gentile converts (Acts 15:7-11).

experiences.significance: In Luke's narrative the Cornelius episode is the decisive step by which non-Jews enter the church as Gentiles, without circumcision, and it underpins the early Christian conviction that faith in Christ crosses ethnic and ritual boundaries. Theologically it is cited in debates on the relation between Spirit reception and water baptism: Pentecostals point to tongues as evidence of the Spirit, sacramental traditions to Peter's insistence on baptism even after the Spirit came. It also shaped later Christian thinking on the food laws and on how Christians relate to Judaism, a legacy that modern scholars and Jewish-Christian dialogue examine critically. Historians debate how far Luke has compressed a longer and messier process, but the story remains a key text for mission across cultures.

experiences.title: The New Prophecy of Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla

place.name: Pepuza, Phrygia (near modern Karayakuplu, Uşak, Turkey)

experiences.account: Paraphrase of the hostile sources preserved by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 5.16-18) and Epiphanius (Panarion 48): in Phrygia a recent convert, Montanus, fell into a frenzied, ecstatic state and began to prophesy in an unusual manner, speaking in the first person as the voice of God; two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, did the same. The oracles called for stricter fasting, readiness for martyrdom and a coming descent of the New Jerusalem at Pepuza. Maximilla is reported to have said that after her there would be no more prophet, but the end.

primarySource.title: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.16-19 (quoting an anonymous anti-Montanist writer and Apollonius)
primarySource.citation: Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 5.16.7-9; Epiphanius, Panarion 48.4; Tertullian, De anima 9

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Asian bishops held synods against the movement and some tried to exorcise the prophetesses. Critics objected less to prophecy itself than to its ecstatic, 'unnatural' form, its claim to supersede apostolic teaching and its failed predictions. In Carthage Tertullian embraced the New Prophecy (c. 207) as the Paraclete's discipline for a mature church.

assessments.text: The early church judged Montanism a false prophecy, a key reason prophecy was tested by conformity to apostolic tradition and the bishops' teaching; the episode helped define the closing of public revelation.

Many Pentecostal historians see the Montanists as partly a charismatic movement suppressed by an institutionalising church, while acknowledging the excesses; others hold them up as a warning against prophecy that claims new doctrine.
Montanism is an early illustration of why continuing revelatory prophecy threatens the sufficiency of Scripture.

Inscriptions and the identification of Pepuza (2000s) show a long-lived Phrygian church with women clergy; nearly all our textual evidence comes from opponents, so the movement's self-understanding is hard to recover.

debates: Ecstatic vs. rational prophecy: early critics argued true prophets did not lose self-control.
Can later prophecy add to apostolic revelation?
Women's leadership: Montanist prophetesses were a key point of attack.
experiences.story:
In the middle of the second century Christianity in the inland regions of Asia Minor was growing among rural and small-town communities in Phrygia and Mysia, a region with strong traditions of ecstatic religion. Churches there were led by bishops and elders, but the memory of the apostolic age, when prophets had spoken in the assembly, was still alive. Prophets such as the daughters of Philip (Acts 21:9) and Quadratus were honoured in Asian church tradition.

Around this time a recent convert named Montanus began to prophesy at a village called Ardabau on the border of Mysia and Phrygia. The dates are disputed: Epiphanius suggests about 156-157, while Eusebius' chronology points to around 172. According to the anonymous anti-Montanist writer quoted by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 5.16), Montanus fell into a kind of frenzy and ecstasy, "raving" and speaking strange things in a way that, the writer insisted, contradicted the custom of the church handed down from the beginning. He was soon joined by two women, Priscilla (or Prisca) and Maximilla, who had left their husbands and also prophesied in ecstasy. Followers called the movement simply "the Prophecy" or "the New Prophecy"; opponents called them Cataphrygians, "those of the Phrygians".

Surviving fragments of the prophets' oracles come mostly from hostile writers, especially Epiphanius, Eusebius and Tertullian, who was sympathetic. In them the Spirit speaks in the first person through the prophet. Montanus is quoted as saying, in effect, that he was a lyre and the Spirit the plectrum, and that the Lord Almighty was speaking in a man. According to Epiphanius, a prophetess (he was unsure whether Priscilla or a later follower named Quintilla) reported that Christ came to her in the form of a woman, clothed in a bright robe, and revealed that Pepuza was a holy place where the heavenly Jerusalem would descend. The prophets called for stricter fasting, discouraged remarriage after a spouse's death and urged readiness for martyrdom rather than flight.

The reaction of church leaders was divided at first but became sharply hostile. Bishops in Asia gathered in what Eusebius describes as among the earliest church synods to examine the new prophecy, and condemned it. Two bishops, Zoticus of Comana and Julian of Apamea, are reported to have tried to examine or exorcise Maximilla but were prevented by her followers. Critics such as Apollonius, Miltiades and Apolinarius of Hierapolis argued that true prophets did not speak in ecstasy or lose control of their minds, that the movement's leaders took money and gifts, and that predictions of war and the end had failed. Maximilla, who died around 179, is reported to have said that after her there would be no more prophecy, but the consummation.

The movement spread beyond Phrygia to Rome, Gaul and North Africa. The martyrs of Lyon in 177 sent letters about it to Rome, apparently urging peace. Tertullian says that a bishop of Rome had at one point recognised the prophecies but withdrew his approval after a certain Praxeas persuaded him otherwise (Against Praxeas 1). In Carthage Tertullian himself, from around 207, embraced the New Prophecy, defending it in works such as On the Soul, On Fasting and On Monogamy; he describes a woman in his congregation who received visions during worship and reported them afterwards. In his view the Paraclete was perfecting church discipline, not changing the rule of faith.

Over the following centuries the Montanists, by now organised as a separate church with their own clergy and a patriarch at Pepuza, were increasingly treated as heretics. Imperial laws from the late fourth century restricted them, and under Justinian in the sixth century they faced severe persecution; John of Ephesus reports destroying their shrine at Pepuza and burning the bones of the founders. A plateau site near Karayakuplu in western Turkey was identified as Pepuza in 2001 by the researchers Peter Lampe and William Tabbernee.

Because almost all information comes from opponents, historians reconstruct the movement with caution. Some see it as a conservative renewal of earlier charismatic and apocalyptic Christianity resisting a church becoming more institutional; others stress its innovations, including claims of new revelation and prominent female prophets.

keyMoments.text: Montanus begins to prophesy in ecstasy at Ardabau on the Mysian-Phrygian border, according to Epiphanius' dating (Eusebius suggests around 172).
Priscilla and Maximilla join Montanus as prophetesses, and Pepuza and Tymion are proclaimed as the place of the coming New Jerusalem.
Bishops in Asia Minor meet in some of the earliest recorded synods and condemn the New Prophecy.
The martyrs of Lyon write to Rome about the movement, reportedly seeking peace among the churches.
Maximilla dies, reportedly having said that no prophet would follow her, only the end.
Tertullian in Carthage openly supports the New Prophecy and defends its stricter discipline.
Under Justinian, John of Ephesus reports destroying the Montanist shrine at Pepuza.
Researchers Peter Lampe and William Tabbernee identify the probable site of Pepuza near Karayakuplu, Turkey.

experiences.significance: The Montanist crisis was one of the first great tests of how the church would judge claims of new prophecy, and the response helped consolidate episcopal authority, synodal decision-making and a sense that public revelation had closed with the apostolic writings. Church historians often link it to the gradual fixing of the New Testament canon and to suspicion of ecstatic speech in later mainstream Christianity. Some modern writers, including Pentecostal and feminist historians, see the Montanists more sympathetically as charismatic and female-led Christians marginalised by an institutionalising church, while critics note their claims of fresh revelation and rigorist discipline. Because our evidence comes mostly from opponents, Montanism remains a classic case study in how history is written by the side that prevails.

experiences.title: Perpetua's prison visions at Carthage
experiences.account: Paraphrase of the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, chs. 3-10, which presents itself as Perpetua's own prison diary: asked by her brother to request a vision, she sees a bronze ladder to heaven guarded by a dragon, climbs it and is welcomed by a shepherd in a garden who gives her cheese-like curd; she later sees her dead brother Dinocrates suffering and, after her prayers, refreshed; on the eve of the games she dreams she is made a man and defeats an Egyptian gladiator, and understands she will fight the devil and win. She and her slave Felicity were executed in the arena on 7 March 203.

primarySource.title: The Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: The editor, possibly sympathetic to the New Prophecy, presents the visions as proof that the Spirit still gives 'new visions' in the last days (Joel 2). Augustine later preached on her feast and felt bound to argue that the Dinocrates vision did not imply salvation for the unbaptised.

assessments.text: Perpetua and Felicity are commemorated in the Roman canon of the Mass; the visions are revered as a martyr's graces, while the Dinocrates vision is cited in debates on prayer for the dead.
Valued as an authentic early witness to costly faith; the prayer-for-the-dead element is usually treated as a historical curiosity rather than doctrine.
Widely accepted as one of the earliest surviving texts by a Christian woman. Scholars debate how much the Montanist-leaning editor shaped it and how to read its dream imagery.
The dreams have been read as a young mother's processing of family conflict, gender and impending death (e.g. the gender reversal in the final vision).

debates: Montanist influence on the text.
Prayer for the dead and the Dinocrates vision.
experiences.story:
Carthage, in Roman North Africa (modern Tunisia), was one of the largest cities of the western empire at the start of the third century and home to a vigorous Christian community. Under the emperor Septimius Severus, local persecution broke out; later sources speak of an imperial ban on conversion to Judaism or Christianity, though historians doubt whether such an edict existed. In 203 a group of catechumens, people still being prepared for baptism, was arrested, perhaps in the nearby town of Thuburbo Minus.

The group included Vibia Perpetua, a well-born married woman of about twenty-two who was nursing an infant son; Felicity, an enslaved woman who was eight months pregnant; Revocatus, also a slave; and two young men, Saturninus and Secundulus. Their teacher, Saturus, was not arrested at first but later gave himself up to share their fate. The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, the account of their imprisonment and death, contains a section that presents itself as Perpetua's own prison diary, written in her own hand, together with a vision narrated by Saturus and a framing introduction and conclusion by an editor. Many scholars accept the diary as genuine, making it one of the earliest surviving texts written by a Christian woman.

Perpetua describes the conditions of prison: the darkness, the heat and crowding, the rough treatment by soldiers, her anxiety for her baby until he was allowed to stay with her. Her father, a pagan, came repeatedly to beg her to sacrifice for his sake and for her child's. She records pointing to a water jug and asking whether it could be called by any name other than what it was; so she, she said, could not call herself anything other than a Christian. Before baptism, which the catechumens received in custody, she wrote that the Spirit told her to ask for nothing from the water except endurance of the flesh.

Her brother urged her to ask for a vision to learn whether they would be freed or would suffer. She records that she saw a bronze ladder reaching to heaven, so narrow that only one person could climb it at a time, with weapons fixed to its sides and a serpent lying at the foot. Saturus climbed first; she trod on the serpent's head and climbed after him into a vast garden, where a tall white-haired man dressed as a shepherd was milking sheep. He welcomed her and gave her a mouthful of curds, and she woke still tasting something sweet. She understood that they would die. In later visions she saw her brother Dinocrates, who had died of a facial cancer at the age of seven, suffering and thirsty, and after praying for him saw him healed and drinking from a golden bowl. The night before the games she saw herself turned into a man, fighting and defeating an Egyptian in the arena, and woke understanding that she would fight against the devil and win.

At the hearing before the procurator Hilarianus, Perpetua refused to sacrifice for the welfare of the emperors and declared herself a Christian. The prisoners were condemned to the beasts at games held for the birthday of the young Caesar Geta, on 7 March 203. Felicity, afraid that her pregnancy would delay her execution, since pregnant women could not be executed, gave birth in prison two days before; the baby girl was taken in by a Christian woman.

The editor describes the day of the games. The prisoners walked into the amphitheatre with joyful faces. The men were set against a leopard, a bear and a boar; Perpetua and Felicity were exposed to a wild cow. Perpetua, tossed, is said to have pinned up her hair and covered her thigh, and to have helped Felicity to her feet. At the end the survivors were killed by the sword. The young gladiator assigned to Perpetua struck badly, and, according to the editor, she herself guided his trembling hand to her throat.

The Passion was read in the churches of North Africa; Augustine preached on the martyrs' feast and warned against treating the account as Scripture. Some scholars detect sympathy for the New Prophecy (Montanism) in the editor's emphasis on new visions, though the point is disputed. Perpetua and Felicity are still commemorated on 7 March, and their names appear in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

keyMoments.text: A group of catechumens including Perpetua, Felicity, Revocatus, Saturninus and Secundulus is arrested in or near Carthage under Septimius Severus.
Perpetua resists her father's pleas to recant and is baptised while in custody.
She records her vision of a narrow bronze ladder, a serpent and a shepherd in a garden, which she takes as a sign that they will die.
Perpetua and the others confess themselves Christians before the procurator Hilarianus and are condemned to the beasts.
Perpetua sees visions of her dead brother Dinocrates and of herself fighting an Egyptian in the arena.
The martyrs die in the amphitheatre of Carthage at games for the birthday of Geta Caesar.
Augustine preaches on the martyrs' feast and cautions against treating their Passion as Scripture.

experiences.significance: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity is one of the most important texts of early Christianity: a rare first-person voice of a young woman, a vivid witness to persecution, and an early record of visionary experience valued by a Christian community. It shaped the cult of the martyrs, the idea of martyrdom as spiritual combat and later Christian reflections on prayer for the dead (through the Dinocrates vision). Historians and feminist scholars study it for gender, family and social status in Roman Africa, and debate how far the editor has shaped it and whether it reflects Montanist sympathies. Perpetua and Felicity remain widely venerated across Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican traditions.

experiences.title: Antony and the Desert Fathers: combat with demons and the flame of prayer

place.name: Inner Mountain (Monastery of St Antony, Eastern Desert of Egypt)

experiences.account: Paraphrase of Athanasius' Life of Antony and the Sayings of the Desert Fathers: after withdrawing into the desert (c. 285), Antony is assailed by demons in the form of beasts and soldiers, and after a long struggle sees the roof open and a beam of light descend, and the pain cease. Emerging after twenty years, he is described as neither emaciated nor overfed, heals the sick and casts out demons. In the Sayings, Abba Joseph answers a monk asking what more he can do by stretching his hands to heaven, his fingers becoming like ten lamps of fire, and saying that he may become all flame.

primarySource.title: Athanasius, Life of Antony
primarySource.citation: Athanasius, Vita Antonii 8-10; 14; Apophthegmata Patrum (alphabetical), Joseph of Panephysis 7

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: For Athanasius, Antony embodies Christ's victory over demons and a life lived in the strength of the incarnate Word; the Life quickly became a bestseller and helped spread monasticism (it features in Augustine's conversion story). The desert tradition was also cautious: many sayings warn monks against seeking visions and against demons appearing as angels of light.

assessments.text: The desert fathers are the root of Orthodox spirituality; their discernment (diakrisis) and stress on humility over visions shape Orthodox caution toward extraordinary experiences.
Antony is the father of monasticism; the Life is read as a classic of spiritual combat, though modern Catholic scholarship recognises its hagiographical style.
The Reformers admired the desert fathers' devotion but rejected monastic vows as a superior way; miracle stories are generally treated as legendary embellishment.
Antony is historical (letters attributed to him survive), but the Life is shaped by Athanasius' anti-Arian and ecclesiastical aims (David Brakke); demon narratives reflect late antique cosmology.

debates: Discernment of spirits: the desert tradition's warnings about deceptive visions.
Historicity of hagiography.
experiences.story:
In the late third century the Roman province of Egypt had many Christians, especially in Alexandria and, increasingly, among Coptic-speaking villagers along the Nile. Individual ascetics already lived on the edges of villages, devoting themselves to prayer, fasting and celibacy. What was new, and what made Antony famous, was the move into the desert itself. Almost everything known about him comes from the Life of Antony written by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, shortly after Antony's death in 356, supplemented by sayings attributed to him in the collections known as the Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum) and by seven letters ascribed to him.

According to Athanasius, Antony was born around 251 to well-off Christian parents in a village in Middle Egypt, traditionally identified as Coma (modern Qiman al-Arus). When he was about eighteen or twenty his parents died, leaving him responsible for a younger sister. Some months later, entering church, he heard the Gospel reading in which Jesus tells the rich young man, "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor" (Matthew 19:21). He took it as addressed to him, gave away his land, placed his sister with a community of virgins and began an ascetic life under the guidance of an old man on the edge of the village.

Athanasius then narrates a series of increasingly radical withdrawals. Antony shut himself in a tomb some distance from the village, where, the Life says, demons attacked him so violently that he was found half-dead; when he recovered he defied them, and a light from above ended the assault. Around 285 he crossed the Nile and lived for about twenty years alone in an abandoned fort at Pispir, the "outer mountain", receiving bread through the wall twice a year. The Life describes his battles with demons in the form of wild beasts, seductive women and mirages of silver and gold, and presents him as winning through prayer, the sign of the cross and humility.

When friends finally broke down the door, around 305, they were amazed, Athanasius says, to find him neither wasted nor bloated, but balanced in body and soul. Disciples gathered around him and the desert, in Athanasius' famous phrase, became a city of monks. During the persecution under Maximinus Daia in 311 Antony went to Alexandria to encourage the martyrs, hoping to be martyred himself. Afterwards, seeking more solitude, he joined a caravan into the Eastern Desert and settled at the "inner mountain" near the Red Sea, where he cultivated a small garden and where the Monastery of St Antony stands today.

The Life attributes to Antony healings, discernment of spirits and foreknowledge of events, and reports that visitors came to him from all classes, including philosophers, whom he answered through an interpreter, as he spoke Coptic. Athanasius stresses Antony's loyalty to the bishops and his opposition to the Arians and Melitians; around 338 Antony is said to have visited Alexandria to support Athanasius' party. He died in 356, said to be about 105 years old, after asking his disciples to bury him in a secret place.

Historians handle the Life with care. Athanasius wrote with clear aims: to offer a model of the monastic life, to claim the famous hermit for Nicene orthodoxy, and to show the triumph of Christ over the demons. The letters attributed to Antony, which many scholars accept, show a more learned figure influenced by Origen's theology, at some distance from the unlettered saint of the Life. Antony was not the first hermit; Jerome even wrote a Life of Paul of Thebes, an earlier hermit, though most historians consider that work largely legendary.

The Life spread rapidly. It was translated into Latin, first anonymously and then by Evagrius of Antioch, and became a model for Christian biography. Augustine's Confessions describe how the story of Antony, told to him and Alypius by Ponticianus in Milan in 386, helped bring about his own conversion.

keyMoments.text: Antony is born to Christian parents in a village in Middle Egypt, according to Athanasius.
After his parents' deaths, Antony hears Matthew 19:21 read in church, gives away his property and begins an ascetic life.
He withdraws across the Nile to a deserted fort at Pispir, where he lives in solitude for about twenty years.
Friends break into his retreat and disciples gather; the desert becomes, in Athanasius' phrase, a city of monks.
Antony visits Alexandria during the persecution of Maximinus to support the confessors.
Seeking greater solitude, he settles at the 'inner mountain' near the Red Sea, the site of today's Monastery of St Antony.
Antony dies, said to be about 105, and is buried in a secret place at his own request.
Athanasius writes the Life of Antony, soon translated into Latin and widely read across the empire.

experiences.significance: Antony became the archetype of the Christian hermit and, through Athanasius' Life, the most influential model for monasticism in East and West; together with Pachomius' communal (cenobitic) monasteries in Upper Egypt, his example launched the desert movement that shaped Christian spirituality, theology and culture for centuries. The Life also set the pattern for hagiography, with its narrative of spiritual combat against demons. Coptic, Orthodox, Catholic and other churches venerate him as the 'father of monks'. Critical historians stress that the Life is a theological and political portrait shaped by Athanasius, that ascetic withdrawal predated Antony, and that the letters suggest a more intellectual figure; Protestant critics from the Reformation on questioned the value of withdrawal from ordinary vocation.

experiences.title: Augustine's conversion in the Milan garden: 'Take up and read'
experiences.account: Confessions 8.12 (trans. E.B. Pusey, 1838, public domain): weeping under a fig tree, Augustine hears from a neighbouring house a child's voice chanting 'Take up and read; take up and read.' He opens the apostle's letters at Romans 13:13-14 and reports that 'by a light as it were of serenity infused into my heart, all the darkness of doubt vanished away.' He was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. Months later at Ostia he and his mother Monica shared a brief contemplative ascent (Confessions 9.10).
experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Augustine himself interprets the voice as a divine command, comparing it to Antony's hearing of the Gospel in church. The Confessions frame the moment as the climax of grace overcoming a divided will.

assessments.text: A classic of grace-wrought conversion valued by both Catholic and Protestant traditions; Luther and Calvin read it as a witness to the priority of grace.
Augustine is honoured as a saint in Orthodoxy but his theology is received with reservations; the conversion story is admired as a personal testimony.

Written about eleven years later (c. 397-400), the account is a carefully crafted literary-theological narrative; scholars (e.g. Pierre Courcelle) debated how literally to take the child's voice, though most accept a real crisis in the garden.
William James used Augustine as a classic case of the 'divided self' resolved in conversion.

debates: How much of the Confessions is literary construction?
Grace and free will: Augustine's conversion as a template for his later anti-Pelagian theology.
experiences.story:
Aurelius Augustinus was born in 354 at Thagaste in Roman North Africa (modern Souk Ahras, Algeria) to a pagan father, Patricius, and a devout Christian mother, Monica. Educated in rhetoric at Madaura and Carthage, he had a brilliant career as a teacher. At nineteen, reading Cicero's now lost Hortensius, he was fired with a love of wisdom; for about nine years he was a 'hearer' among the Manichaeans, who taught a dualism of light and darkness. He lived with a woman whose name he never gives, and they had a son, Adeodatus. In 384 he obtained the prestigious post of official rhetor in Milan, then an imperial residence.

His Confessions, written around 397-400 as a long prayer addressed to God, are the main source for what followed. In Milan he began to listen to the sermons of Bishop Ambrose, at first for their style, and found that Ambrose's allegorical reading of the Old Testament answered some Manichaean objections. Reading 'books of the Platonists' (probably Plotinus and Porphyry in Latin translation) helped him conceive of God as immaterial and of evil as a lack of good rather than a substance. Yet, as he describes it, he remained bound by ambition and especially by sexual desire. Monica arranged a socially suitable marriage, and his long-term partner was sent back to Africa; he took another mistress while waiting.

In Book 8 Augustine tells of the summer of 386. The elderly priest Simplicianus told him how the famous Roman rhetor Marius Victorinus had publicly professed Christianity. Then a visitor from Africa, Ponticianus, an official at the court, noticed a copy of Paul's letters on Augustine's table and told him and his friend Alypius about Antony of Egypt and about two court officials at Trier who had abandoned their careers after reading the Life of Antony. Augustine describes himself as shaken and ashamed: unlearned people were seizing heaven while he and his learning wallowed in flesh and blood.

He went out into the garden of the house where they were staying, followed by Alypius. There, he writes, he struggled with himself, his old desires seeming to pluck at his garment of flesh, while the figure of Continence invited him to trust God. He threw himself down under a fig tree and wept, asking how long it would be "tomorrow, and tomorrow". Then he heard from a neighbouring house a voice, like that of a boy or girl, repeating in a sing-song way, "Tolle lege, tolle lege", "Take up and read, take up and read." He could not remember any children's game with such words. Recalling that Antony had been converted by a Gospel reading heard as addressed to him, he went back, picked up the book of Paul's letters and read the first passage his eyes fell on: "not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof" (Romans 13:13-14, KJV). He writes that at once, as if a light of peace had flooded his heart, all the darkness of doubt vanished.

Alypius read the following verse, 'Him that is weak in the faith receive ye', applied it to himself and joined Augustine's resolution. They went in and told Monica, who rejoiced. Augustine resigned his teaching post at the end of the term, citing chest problems, and retired with friends and family to a country estate at Cassiciacum, where he wrote philosophical dialogues. At the Easter Vigil of 387 he, Alypius and Adeodatus were baptised by Ambrose in Milan. Shortly afterwards, at Ostia, waiting to sail for Africa, he and Monica shared a contemplative experience he describes in Book 9; she died there days later.

Back in Africa, Augustine founded a small community at Thagaste, was ordained priest at Hippo Regius in 391, almost against his will, and became its bishop around 395-396, serving until his death in 430. Historians have debated how literally to take the garden scene. In 1950 Pierre Courcelle argued that elements such as the fig tree and the voice are literary and symbolic; others note that the earlier dialogues from Cassiciacum present his conversion more as a turn to philosophy. Most accept that a decisive crisis happened in Milan in 386, while recognising that the Confessions shape it, years later, into a theological narrative of grace.

keyMoments.text: Augustine is born at Thagaste in North Africa to Patricius and Monica.
Reading Cicero's Hortensius awakens his love of wisdom, and he joins the Manichaeans as a hearer.
He becomes official rhetor in Milan and begins listening to Bishop Ambrose's sermons.
Simplicianus tells him of Victorinus' conversion and Ponticianus tells him of Antony of Egypt.
In a Milan garden he hears a child's voice say 'Take up and read', reads Romans 13:13-14 and resolves to live as a Christian.
Augustine, Alypius and Adeodatus are baptised by Ambrose at the Easter Vigil in Milan; Monica dies soon after at Ostia.
Augustine is ordained priest at Hippo Regius, becoming its bishop around 395-396.
He begins writing the Confessions, which tell the story of his conversion as a prayer to God.

experiences.significance: Augustine's conversion, through the Confessions, became the classic Western account of the restless heart finding rest in God and of grace overcoming a divided will. It shaped Augustine's later theology of sin, grace and predestination, which in turn deeply influenced medieval Catholic thought, Luther, Calvin and the Jansenists. The Confessions also founded the genre of spiritual autobiography and influenced Western ideas of the self and inner life. Eastern Orthodox theologians have often been more reserved about Augustine's views on original sin and grace, and modern scholars debate how far the garden scene is shaped by literary convention, but its influence on Christian and secular culture remains enormous.

experiences.title: Symeon the New Theologian's visions of divine light
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Symeon's Catechetical Discourses (esp. 22), where he describes himself in the third person as a young man named George: praying at night, he is suddenly flooded with a divine light that fills the room; he loses awareness of the walls and of himself, and is filled with tears and joy. In his Hymns of Divine Love he speaks repeatedly of seeing Christ as light and insists that those who say no one can now experience God consciously deny the gospel.

primarySource.title: Symeon the New Theologian, Catechetical Discourses and Hymns of Divine Love
primarySource.citation: Catechesis 22; Hymns of Divine Love (e.g. Hymn 25)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Symeon's claims and his veneration of his own spiritual father caused conflict with church authorities; he was exiled from Constantinople c. 1009 but later rehabilitated. Orthodoxy came to call him 'New Theologian', one of only three so titled (with John the Evangelist and Gregory of Nazianzus).

assessments.text: A canonical teacher of the conscious experience of grace; his insistence that the Spirit's indwelling is felt, not just believed, anticipates hesychasm.
Respected as an Eastern mystic; Catholic theology generally distinguishes such experience from the created grace it posits, a difference sharpened later in the Palamite debate.

Some charismatic writers point to Symeon's 'baptism in the Spirit' language (tears, experiential certainty) as an Eastern parallel to Spirit baptism, while Orthodox scholars caution against equating the two.
His conflict with Stephen of Nicomedia illustrates the perennial tension between charismatic authority and ecclesiastical office in Byzantium.

debates: Charism vs. office: can an unordained or junior monk bind or loose by spiritual authority?
Is conscious experience of grace normal for all Christians?
experiences.story:
In the tenth century Constantinople was the capital of a revived Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian dynasty, and its church was confident, wealthy and highly organised. Monasteries such as the Stoudios monastery were centres of liturgy and learning. Some critics felt that spiritual life had become routine: many assumed that the vivid experience of the Holy Spirit known to the early saints belonged to the past. The monk later called Symeon the New Theologian challenged that assumption with his own experience.

Symeon was born in 949 in Paphlagonia, in northern Asia Minor, to a family of provincial nobility, and was baptised George. As a boy he was sent to Constantinople for education and entered a career at the imperial court. At around fourteen he came under the influence of an elderly monk of Stoudios, Symeon the Studite (also called Eulabes, 'the Pious'), who became his spiritual father. The younger man continued in public life but followed a rule of prayer and reading his elder gave him, including the works of Mark the Hermit.

In his Catechetical Discourses (especially Discourse 22) Symeon describes, in the third person, the experience of a young man named George, generally accepted as himself, when he was about twenty. One evening while praying, he wrote, a divine light suddenly shone down from above and filled the room. The young man lost awareness of where he was and seemed to himself to be all light, filled with tears and joy. In the light he saw what seemed like a cloud, and next to it his spiritual father. The experience faded, and George, by his own account, fell back into a careless life for some years.

Around 977 he entered Stoudios as a novice, taking the name Symeon, but tension arose over his intense devotion to his elder, and he moved to the small monastery of St Mamas in the capital. He was ordained priest and around 980 became its abbot, serving for about twenty-five years. In his Hymns of Divine Love and his discourses he described repeated experiences of the uncreated light, which he identified with God himself, and insisted that anyone who had not consciously experienced the Holy Spirit was not yet fully a Christian. He spoke frankly of tears, of seeing Christ as light and of a personal relationship with God, in language that many found startling.

His teaching provoked resistance. Some monks at St Mamas rebelled against his demanding regime. More seriously, he clashed with Stephen, former metropolitan of Nicomedia and a learned official of the patriarchate, partly over Symeon's public veneration of his spiritual father, Symeon the Studite, as a saint, with an icon and feast, without official approval. Symeon also argued that spiritual authority, including the power to hear confessions and bind and loose, belonged to those who had experienced the Spirit, not only to the ordained. In 1009 he was exiled across the Bosphorus, where he settled at a ruined chapel of St Marina near Paloukiton and formed a new community. He was later rehabilitated but chose to stay, dying there in 1022.

His disciple Niketas Stethatos wrote his Life and edited his works. Symeon's emphasis on conscious experience of divine light was later taken up by the hesychast monks of Mount Athos, and his works were included in part in the Philokalia. He is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church, which gives the title 'Theologian' to only two others: John the Evangelist and Gregory of Nazianzus.

keyMoments.text: Symeon, baptised George, is born in Paphlagonia to a provincial noble family.
As a youth in Constantinople he takes the Studite monk Symeon the Pious as his spiritual father.
Around the age of twenty he experiences an overwhelming vision of divine light while praying, later described in Catechetical Discourse 22.
He enters the Stoudios monastery and soon moves to the monastery of St Mamas.
He becomes abbot of St Mamas, writing discourses and hymns about the experience of divine light.
After conflict with Stephen of Nicomedia and others, Symeon is exiled across the Bosphorus and founds a new community.
Symeon dies in exile; his disciple Niketas Stethatos later writes his Life and edits his works.

experiences.significance: Symeon is a pivotal figure in Byzantine mysticism, insisting that conscious experience of God as light is available and essential to Christian life, not merely a memory of the apostolic age. His ideas helped prepare the hesychast tradition and Gregory Palamas' theology of the uncreated light, and he remains central to Orthodox spirituality through the Philokalia. His claim that spiritual authority rests on experience of the Spirit raised lasting questions about charisma and church office, questions that also interest Protestant, Pentecostal and charismatic readers who see in him an Eastern witness to Spirit-filled experience. Critics, then and now, have warned that his approach could undermine ecclesial order or encourage subjective claims.

experiences.title: Hesychasm and the uncreated light of Tabor
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Gregory Palamas' Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts (1338-41): monks practising stillness (hesychia), with the Jesus Prayer and controlled breathing, report seeing an ineffable light. Palamas argues this is not a created or symbolic light but the same uncreated divine light that shone from Christ at the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor (Matthew 17:2): the energies of God, in which humans truly participate, while God's essence remains unknowable.

primarySource.title: Gregory Palamas, Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: The Calabrian monk Barlaam mocked the hesychasts as 'navel-gazers' (omphalopsychoi) and argued any light seen must be created. Councils at Constantinople (1341, 1347, 1351) upheld Palamas; he became Archbishop of Thessalonica and was canonised in 1368.

assessments.text: The essence-energies distinction is dogmatic for most Orthodox theologians: deification (theosis) is real participation in God's uncreated energies, and the light of Tabor is its foretaste. The second Sunday of Lent honours Palamas.

Historically many Western theologians judged the essence-energies distinction a compromise of divine simplicity; since the 20th century many Catholic scholars see it as compatible with, or complementary to, Thomist teaching.
Generally unfamiliar until recently; some Reformed critics share the divine-simplicity objection, while others see parallels with union-with-Christ theology.

The breathing technique and light visions have been compared with Sufi dhikr and other contemplative methods; the controversy was also bound up with Byzantine civil war politics (Kantakouzenos vs. the regency).

debates: Essence vs. energies and divine simplicity.
Is the light created or uncreated?
Psychosomatic prayer methods: legitimate aid or mechanical technique?
experiences.story:
By the early fourteenth century Mount Athos, the monastic peninsula in northern Greece, was the spiritual heart of the Byzantine world, even as the empire itself shrank under pressure from Serbs, Latins and Ottoman Turks. Among its monks a method of prayer called hesychasm (from hesychia, stillness) had become widespread. Building on a long tradition reaching back to the desert fathers, John Climacus and Symeon the New Theologian, hesychasts repeated the Jesus Prayer ('Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me') continuously, sometimes with a bodily technique: sitting with head bowed, controlling the breath and focusing attention on the heart. Teachers such as Gregory of Sinai (d. 1346) taught that through such prayer a purified monk might behold the divine light, the same light that shone from Christ at his Transfiguration on Mount Tabor (Matthew 17:1-8).

Gregory Palamas, born around 1296 into a noble family close to the imperial court, had renounced a promising career to become a monk on Athos around 1316. He lived for years in hesychast practice, at times in a hermitage near Veroia and at the Great Lavra, and was ordained priest. By the 1330s he was a respected spiritual teacher.

The controversy began with Barlaam of Calabria, a learned Greek-speaking monk from southern Italy who had come to Constantinople and become a leading theologian, active in negotiations with Latin envoys. Around 1336-1337 Barlaam encountered hesychast monks and was scandalised. He mocked them as omphalopsychoi, 'people with their souls in their navels', and argued that God is unknowable in himself, so that any light seen by the eyes must be either a created symbol or an illusion. To claim to see God's own light, he held, was to fall into the error of the Messalians, an ancient sect accused of claiming visible experience of God.

Palamas responded in a series of treatises, the Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts, written around 1338-1341. He argued that God is indeed utterly unknowable in his essence, but that he truly makes himself known and shared in his uncreated energies, his activities or operations, which are God himself acting, not created intermediaries. The light seen by the apostles on Tabor, and by the saints in prayer, is therefore uncreated, a real participation in God, though not in the divine essence. On the body, he insisted that since Christ took flesh and the body is a temple of the Spirit, it can share in prayer and be transfigured. In 1340-1341 the leading monks of Athos signed the Hagioretic Tome endorsing his position.

A synod met in Constantinople in June 1341, in the church of Hagia Sophia, under Emperor Andronikos III, and found against Barlaam, who soon left for Italy and later became a Catholic bishop. But the emperor died days later, and the theological dispute became entangled in a civil war between the regency for the young John V and John Kantakouzenos. A new critic, Gregory Akindynos, attacked Palamas' distinction between essence and energies as introducing two divinities; Palamas was imprisoned and excommunicated under Patriarch John Kalekas. After Kantakouzenos' victory, councils in 1347 and 1351 vindicated Palamas, while the scholar Nikephoros Gregoras continued to oppose him. Palamas became archbishop of Thessalonica in 1347, was captured by the Ottomans in 1354 and held for about a year, and died in 1359. He was proclaimed a saint in 1368.

Historians note that the dispute was about more than a prayer method: it involved the relation of philosophy to revelation, the knowability of God and how humans can be 'deified' (theosis). Some modern Western scholars, both Catholic and Protestant, long regarded Palamism as a Byzantine innovation that compromised divine simplicity, while twentieth-century Orthodox theologians such as Vladimir Lossky and John Meyendorff presented it as the authentic expression of patristic tradition.

keyMoments.text: Gregory Palamas becomes a monk on Mount Athos, where hesychast prayer is widespread.
Barlaam of Calabria encounters hesychast monks and attacks their method and claims to see divine light.
Palamas begins writing the Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts, distinguishing God's essence from his uncreated energies.
Leading Athonite monks endorse Palamas' teaching in the Hagioretic Tome.
A council in Constantinople condemns Barlaam, but civil war soon reopens the controversy.
After John Kantakouzenos' victory a council vindicates Palamas, who becomes archbishop of Thessalonica.
A further council in Constantinople confirms the essence-energies distinction as Orthodox teaching.
Nine years after his death, Gregory Palamas is proclaimed a saint by the Patriarch Philotheos Kokkinos.

experiences.significance: The hesychast controversy fixed the essence-energies distinction and the doctrine of deification through participation in the uncreated light as defining features of Eastern Orthodox theology. It gave lasting legitimacy to the Jesus Prayer and contemplative monasticism, transmitted later through the Philokalia (1782) to Russia and to modern readers worldwide. It also widened the theological distance between Byzantium and the Latin West just as union negotiations were under way, and Western theologians long criticised Palamism as compromising God's simplicity, a judgement many Catholic scholars have since softened. Today Gregory Palamas is commemorated on the Second Sunday of Lent in the Orthodox Church.

experiences.title: Hildegard of Bingen's 'living light'
experiences.account: Paraphrase of the Protestificatio (preface) of Scivias: in 1141, when she was forty-two years and seven months old, a fiery light of great brilliance came from the open heavens and poured into her whole brain and heart, and she suddenly understood the meaning of the Psalter, the Gospels and the other Scriptures. She insists she saw these things not in dreams, sleep or frenzy but awake, with the eyes and ears of the inner self. Later she described a lesser 'shadow of the living light' that was always with her.

primarySource.title: Hildegard of Bingen, Scivias (Know the Ways), 1141-51
primarySource.citation: Scivias, Protestificatio; Letter to Guibert of Gembloux (1175)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Hildegard wrote to Bernard of Clairvaux for reassurance, and Pope Eugenius III had parts of Scivias read at the Synod of Trier (1147-48) and encouraged her to continue writing, giving her unusual authority to preach and correspond with emperors and popes as a prophetess.

assessments.text: Canonised (equivalent canonisation) and declared a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XVI in 2012; her visions are regarded as authentic private revelation integrated into sound theology.
Often valued as a creative theologian, composer and naturalist, and as an example of a woman's prophetic voice, without accepting all her visionary claims as revelation.

Charles Singer (1917) and Oliver Sacks suggested her descriptions of light and fortification-like patterns resemble migraine aura; this does not settle the religious question of meaning, as Sacks himself noted.
Her visionary authority let a woman speak publicly in a church that barred women from preaching; scholars such as Barbara Newman stress how she navigated this 'prophetic' role.

debates: Migraine hypothesis and naturalistic explanation.
Women's authority through visionary prophecy.
experiences.story:
In twelfth-century Germany monasteries were powerful centres of learning and economic life, and the Church was in the midst of reform movements and controversies over papal and imperial authority. Women's religious life was usually attached to male houses. Hildegard was born in 1098 at Bermersheim, in the Rhineland, the tenth child of a noble family. As a child she was offered to the religious life and, around 1112, was enclosed with Jutta of Sponheim, a young noblewoman anchoress, in a cell attached to the Benedictine monastery of Disibodenberg. A small community of women formed around them.

Hildegard later wrote that she had seen visions from early childhood, a light she called 'the reflection of the living Light', but had told almost no one, fearing ridicule. When Jutta died in 1136, Hildegard was chosen to lead the women's community. In 1141, at the age of forty-two years and seven months, according to the preface of her book Scivias ('Know the Ways'), she experienced a fiery light of great brilliance coming from the open heavens that poured into her whole brain and inflamed her heart, and she suddenly understood the meaning of the Scriptures. She reports a command to write down what she saw and heard. She insisted that she saw these things not in dreams or ecstasy but wide awake, with the eyes and ears of the inner self.

At first, she wrote, she refused out of doubt and humility, and fell seriously ill. Encouraged by the monk Volmar, her teacher and secretary, and by the abbot Kuno, she began writing. Scivias, completed about ten years later, describes twenty-six visions: images of the cosmos as an egg, of the Church as a woman, of the Trinity, of the fall and of the end of history, each followed by a lengthy explanation in the voice of the 'Living Light'. The manuscript produced at Rupertsberg (lost in 1945 but preserved in photographs and a hand-made copy) included striking illuminations of the visions.

Needing approval, around 1146-1147 Hildegard wrote to Bernard of Clairvaux, the most influential churchman of the age, asking whether she should speak or keep silent; Bernard replied briefly with encouragement. At the synod of Trier in 1147-1148, Pope Eugenius III, himself a Cistercian, had portions of Scivias read aloud, and, according to her Life, sent her a letter approving her work and encouraging her to continue. From then on she was widely recognised as a prophetess, the 'Sibyl of the Rhine'.

Against the opposition of the Disibodenberg monks, who stood to lose her community's dowries and prestige, Hildegard moved her nuns around 1150 to a new foundation at Rupertsberg near Bingen, again after an illness she interpreted as a sign of God's displeasure at the delay. There she wrote two more visionary books, the Book of Life's Merits and the Book of Divine Works, as well as medical and natural-history works, a cycle of liturgical songs, the music drama Ordo Virtutum and some 300 letters to popes, emperors, bishops and lay people. Unusually for a woman, she undertook preaching tours in the Rhineland, denouncing clerical corruption and the Cathars.

In her last years she faced conflict when she buried in her community's cemetery a nobleman who had been excommunicated, insisting he had been reconciled; the clergy of Mainz placed the convent under interdict in 1178, forbidding music and sacraments, until it was lifted shortly before her death on 17 September 1179. Her cult continued locally, and she was long venerated as a saint in Germany; in 2012 Pope Benedict XVI formally extended her veneration to the universal Church and named her a Doctor of the Church.

Modern readers have proposed various explanations of her visions. The historian of medicine Charles Singer suggested in 1917, and the neurologist Oliver Sacks later popularised the view, that features of her descriptions, such as points of light and fortification patterns, resemble migraine aura. Others warn that a neurological description, even if correct, does not settle the religious or intellectual meaning she gave the experiences.

keyMoments.text: Hildegard is born at Bermersheim in the Rhineland to a noble family.
She is enclosed with Jutta of Sponheim at the monastery of Disibodenberg.
After Jutta's death Hildegard becomes leader of the women's community.
At forty-two she experiences a fiery light and a command to write, and begins Scivias with the help of the monk Volmar.
Hildegard writes to Bernard of Clairvaux, and at the synod of Trier (1147-1148) Pope Eugenius III has parts of Scivias read aloud.
She moves her nuns to a new convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen.
Scivias is completed, followed by further visionary, scientific, musical and epistolary works.
Her convent is placed under interdict after she buries an excommunicated nobleman.
Hildegard dies at Rupertsberg; in 2012 she is canonised for the universal Church and named a Doctor of the Church.

experiences.significance: Hildegard showed that visionary experience could give a twelfth-century woman an authoritative public voice in theology, church reform, medicine and music, at a time when women were otherwise excluded from teaching. Her papal approval set a precedent for later female visionaries and for the Church's practice of testing and authorising private revelations. She is studied today as a theologian, composer and naturalist, and has become a figure of interest for feminist scholarship, ecological spirituality and early music revival, sometimes in ways historians consider anachronistic. Debates about neurological explanations of her visions illustrate wider questions about how to interpret religious experience.

experiences.title: Francis of Assisi receives the stigmata at La Verna
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Thomas of Celano (First Life, 1229) and Bonaventure (Major Legend 13): around the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) 1224, while fasting on Mount La Verna, Francis sees a seraph with six wings, fixed to a cross. As the vision fades, marks like nails appear in his hands and feet and a wound in his side. Brother Elias' letter announcing Francis' death (1226) is the earliest text to mention the marks.

primarySource.title: Thomas of Celano, First Life of St Francis; Bonaventure, Legenda Maior
primarySource.citation: Celano, Vita prima 94-95; Bonaventure, Legenda Maior 13.3; Letter of Elias of Cortona (1226); Francis' autograph 'Chartula' blessing for Brother Leo

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Contemporaries took the stigmata as a seal showing Francis as an 'alter Christus'. Some Dominicans and secular clergy questioned the claim; Pope Gregory IX issued bulls (1237) defending it. It is generally considered the first reported case of stigmata.

assessments.text: The stigmata are commemorated in a feast (17 September) and widely accepted as a supernatural grace, though the Church does not require belief in them.
Orthodox tradition has no stigmatics and is reserved about the phenomenon, seeing a Western emphasis on imitating Christ's physical suffering that differs from Eastern stress on transfiguration.
Usually doubtful or agnostic; Francis is widely admired for poverty and peacemaking, but the stigmata are often attributed to pious embellishment.
