Elias' early letter and multiple witnesses make the claim of visible marks well attested as a belief; explanations range from genuine wounds of unknown cause to self-inflicted or psychosomatic wounds or later elaboration (André Vauchez discusses the sources).

debates: Authenticity and possible natural causes of stigmata.
Why stigmata appear almost exclusively in Latin Catholicism after 1224.
experiences.story:
Francis of Assisi (born Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone around 1181-1182) was the son of a wealthy cloth merchant in Umbria. After a youth of ambition and a spell as a prisoner of war, he underwent a gradual conversion around 1205-1206: he embraced lepers, rebuilt ruined churches and renounced his inheritance before the bishop of Assisi. Followers gathered around his life of radical poverty, preaching and penance, and Pope Innocent III gave verbal approval to their way of life around 1209-1210. By the 1220s the Order of Friars Minor numbered thousands, and Francis, worn out by illness and troubled by the order's institutional growth, had handed over its day-to-day government.

La Verna is a wooded mountain in the Casentino region of Tuscany. In 1213 Count Orlando of Chiusi gave it to Francis as a place of retreat. In the late summer of 1224 Francis went there with a few close companions, among them Brother Leo, to keep a forty-day fast in honour of St Michael the Archangel, from the feast of the Assumption (15 August) to Michaelmas (29 September).

According to Thomas of Celano's First Life of Francis, written in 1228-1229, about two years before his death Francis saw in a vision a man like a seraph with six wings, standing above him with hands outstretched and feet joined, fixed to a cross. Two wings were raised above his head, two spread for flight and two covered his body. Francis was filled with joy at the seraph's gracious look and with sorrow at the crucifixion, and while he was wondering what it meant, the marks of nails began to appear in his hands and feet, and a wound in his right side, which often bled. Later accounts, especially Bonaventure's Major Legend (1260-1263), place the vision around the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, 14 September 1224, and identify the seraph as Christ himself.

Francis tried to conceal the wounds, keeping his hands covered and wearing shoes, and only a few companions saw them during his life. On La Verna he wrote on a small piece of parchment the Praises of God and a blessing for Brother Leo; this 'chartula', one of only two autographs of Francis that survive, is preserved in Assisi, and Leo's notes on it link its writing to the vision of the seraph and the imprinting of the stigmata. Francis came down from the mountain and, though increasingly ill and nearly blind, composed the Canticle of Brother Sun in 1225.

Francis died at the Portiuncula near Assisi on the evening of 3 October 1226. Brother Elias of Cortona, the order's vicar, immediately sent a circular letter announcing that Francis had borne the marks of Christ's passion, describing them as nails formed of his flesh. Witnesses who examined the body, according to Celano and other early sources, described black nail-like formations in the hands and feet and a red wound in the side. Francis was canonised by Pope Gregory IX on 16 July 1228, less than two years after his death.

The stigmata were contested from the start. Some clergy, including a bishop in Moravia and members of rival orders, doubted or denied them, and Gregory IX issued bulls in 1237 defending their authenticity. Bonaventure's Legend, adopted by the Franciscan order in 1266 as its official life, made the stigmata the climax of Francis' identification with Christ.

Modern historians have weighed several possibilities: genuine supernatural marks, as Catholic tradition holds; self-inflicted wounds, conscious or unconscious; a psychosomatic phenomenon; or a later embellishment of signs of illness, such as the leprosy he may have contracted. Some scholars have also noted that Francis' early followers had strong reasons to present him as an alter Christus. The documentary evidence, including Elias' letter and Leo's note, shows at least that the claim was made within days of his death by people who knew him.

keyMoments.text: Francis of Assisi renounces his inheritance and begins a life of poverty and penance.
Count Orlando of Chiusi gives Francis the mountain of La Verna in Tuscany as a place of retreat.
Francis begins a forty-day fast on La Verna in honour of St Michael with Brother Leo and other companions.
According to his early biographers, Francis sees a crucified six-winged seraph and receives wounds in his hands, feet and side.
Francis writes the Praises of God and a blessing for Brother Leo on a parchment still kept in Assisi.
Francis dies at the Portiuncula, and Brother Elias announces in a circular letter that he bore the marks of the Passion.
Pope Gregory IX canonises Francis, and Thomas of Celano writes the First Life describing the stigmata.
Bonaventure completes the Major Legend, which becomes the order's official account of the stigmata.

experiences.significance: Francis' stigmata are the first widely reported case of the phenomenon in Christian history and set a pattern for hundreds of later stigmatics, from Catherine of Siena to Padre Pio. They became central to Franciscan identity and to late medieval devotion to Christ's suffering humanity, influencing art (Giotto's frescoes in Assisi among many others) and piety. Protestant reformers were sceptical of such marvels, and modern historians debate whether the stigmata were miraculous, psychosomatic, self-inflicted or partly hagiographic constructions. The episode remains a key case in the study of religious experience, the body and sanctity.

experiences.title: Catherine of Siena: mystical espousal and invisible stigmata
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Raymond of Capua's Legenda Maior: Catherine experienced a 'mystical marriage' to Christ (c. 1368) and, at Pisa on 1 April 1375, after communion, rays from the crucified Christ pierced her hands, feet and side; at her prayer the wounds remained invisible, causing pain but no marks. Her disciples recorded her dictating The Dialogue while in ecstasy (1377-78).

primarySource.title: Raymond of Capua, Life of Catherine of Siena; Catherine, The Dialogue
primarySource.citation: Raymond of Capua, Legenda Maior 2.6 (stigmata); The Dialogue (1378)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Her ecstatic authority lent weight to her letters urging Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome (1376-77). Franciscans contested Dominican claims of her stigmata; Pope Sixtus IV (a Franciscan) at one point forbade depicting them.

assessments.text: Saint, Doctor of the Church (1970) and co-patron of Europe; her mystical experiences are treated as authentic graces, though the invisible-stigmata claim is not a matter of faith.
Admired for courageous church reform and social service; extreme fasting and ecstatic claims are often viewed critically.
Caroline Walker Bynum interprets her extreme fasting and eucharistic piety as a form of female religious agency; Raymond's Life is hagiography written to support canonisation.
Her refusal of food has been debated as 'holy anorexia' (Rudolph Bell), a diagnosis others reject as anachronistic.

debates: Female mystics, fasting and authority.
Rivalry between religious orders over stigmata claims.
experiences.story:
Fourteenth-century Italy was shaken by plague, by wars between city-states and by the absence of the popes, who had lived at Avignon since 1309. Catherine Benincasa was born in Siena in 1347, the year before the Black Death reached the city, one of the youngest of a very large family; her father Jacopo was a wool dyer. According to her confessor and biographer Raymond of Capua, she saw a vision of Christ above the church of San Domenico when she was about six and soon after vowed virginity. She resisted her family's plans for her marriage, cut off her hair and was eventually allowed to join the Mantellate, a group of mostly widowed Dominican tertiaries who lived at home, around 1363-1364.

For about three years she lived in near seclusion in a small room in her family's house, praying, fasting and sleeping little. Around 1367-1368 she experienced what Raymond describes as a mystical marriage to Christ, who gave her a ring visible only to herself. Soon after, she reported, Christ told her to go out and serve others. She began nursing the sick and plague victims, caring for prisoners and the poor, and gathered a circle of followers, men and women, clerics and lay people, who called her 'mamma'. Her extreme fasting became notorious: Raymond reports that for long periods she could take little or nothing but the Eucharist, and critics accused her of hypocrisy or pride.

On 1 April 1375, while visiting Pisa, Catherine received communion in the little church of Santa Cristina. According to Raymond, who was present and wrote the account a decade or more later, she fell into ecstasy and afterwards told him that she had seen the crucified Lord coming toward her in great light, and that rays of blood-red light came from the five wounds toward her hands, feet and heart. She asked that the marks not be visible, and the rays, she said, turned to pure light before reaching her. She reported feeling the pain of the wounds for the rest of her life. According to Raymond, the marks became visible on her body only after her death.

Catherine's influence grew far beyond Siena. She dictated hundreds of letters (about 380 survive) to popes, rulers, mercenary captains and ordinary people. In 1376 she travelled to Avignon to plead with Pope Gregory XI to return to Rome and to make peace with Florence. Gregory did return in January 1377, though historians debate how decisive her influence was. In 1377-1378 she dictated her major work, the Dialogue, a conversation between the soul and God on discernment, providence, obedience and prayer, written partly while in ecstasy according to her disciples.

When the Great Western Schism broke out in 1378, with rival popes in Rome and Avignon, Catherine supported Urban VI and moved to Rome to work for him. Exhausted by fasting and grief at the divided Church, she died there on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three. Raymond of Capua, later master general of the Dominicans, wrote her Legenda maior to promote her canonisation, which Pope Pius II, himself a Sienese, proclaimed in 1461.

Her stigmata were disputed, especially by Franciscans, who regarded the stigmata as a unique privilege of Francis; Pope Sixtus IV, a Franciscan, is reported to have forbidden depictions of her with visible wounds, and artists often showed rays instead. Modern historians have also discussed her fasting in light of what Rudolph Bell called 'holy anorexia' (1985), a reading others criticise as projecting a modern diagnosis onto a different religious culture. In 1970 Paul VI named her one of the first two women Doctors of the Church, together with Teresa of Ávila, and in 1999 John Paul II made her a co-patron of Europe.

keyMoments.text: Catherine Benincasa is born in Siena, the daughter of a wool dyer.
After resisting marriage she is admitted to the Mantellate, a group of Dominican tertiaries living at home.
Following years of seclusion she experiences a 'mystical marriage' to Christ and turns to public service of the sick and poor.
In the church of Santa Cristina in Pisa she reports receiving invisible stigmata as rays from Christ's wounds.
She travels to Avignon to urge Pope Gregory XI to return to Rome and make peace with Florence.
She dictates the Dialogue and, after the Western Schism begins, supports Urban VI in Rome.
Catherine dies in Rome at thirty-three; Raymond of Capua later writes her Legenda maior.
Pope Pius II canonises Catherine; in 1970 she is named a Doctor of the Church.

experiences.significance: Catherine of Siena showed how a laywoman without formal education could, through a reputation for mystical experience, exercise remarkable public authority in church politics, diplomacy and spiritual teaching. Her Dialogue and letters are classics of Italian literature and Catholic spirituality, and her example shaped later models of active, apostolic holiness for women. Her stigmata, and the dispute with Franciscans over them, show how claims of mystical favour were contested along institutional lines. Modern scholars debate her fasting, the role of Raymond of Capua in shaping her image and the extent of her political influence, while Catholics honour her as a Doctor of the Church and patron of Italy and Europe.

experiences.title: Julian of Norwich's sixteen 'showings'
experiences.account: Paraphrase with short quotation from Revelations of Divine Love (Long Text): at thirty and a half years old, on 8 or 13 May 1373, gravely ill and given the last rites, Julian gazes at a crucifix and receives sixteen 'showings' over a night and day: the bleeding head of Christ, a hazelnut-sized thing representing 'all that is made', and Christ telling her that sin is 'behovely' and that 'all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' (ch. 27). She recovers, and spends some twenty years reflecting on their meaning, including Christ as Mother.

primarySource.title: Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love (Short and Long Texts)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Julian lived as an anchoress at St Julian's church, Norwich. Margery Kempe records consulting her about discernment of her own visions (c. 1413), and Julian advised testing whether they led to charity and conformity with the faith.

assessments.text: Venerated (her feast is kept locally) and widely read; her optimism about divine love is admired, while some theologians ask how her near-universal hope fits Church teaching on judgement.
Commemorated on 8 May in the Church of England; often treated as a mother of English spiritual writing.
Appreciated for devotion to the cross; some critics question the 'Christ as Mother' imagery and hints of universalism.
Her texts are well documented (manuscripts c. 15th-17th c.); the Short Text may date from the 1380s, the Long from the 1390s-1410s. Her illness-and-recovery narrative is plausibly autobiographical.

debates: Universal salvation hints ('all shall be well').
Feminine imagery for God.
Discernment criteria for private revelation.
experiences.story:
Norwich in the late fourteenth century was one of the largest and richest cities in England, a centre of the wool trade with dozens of parish churches, a cathedral priory and many religious houses. It was also a place of suffering: the Black Death had struck in 1348-1349 and returned several times; the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was put down harshly by Bishop Henry Despenser; and from the 1390s Lollards, followers of John Wycliffe, were tried and later burned at the Lollards' Pit just outside the city. Against this background a woman whose own name is unknown wrote the earliest surviving book in English known to be by a woman.

We know her as Julian because she later lived as an anchoress, enclosed in a cell attached to the church of St Julian at Conisford in Norwich. Almost all information comes from her own book, known as Revelations of Divine Love or the Showings. She says that as a young woman she had asked God for three gifts: a vivid understanding of Christ's passion, a bodily sickness bringing her close to death, and three 'wounds' of contrition, compassion and longing for God.

In May 1373, when she was thirty and a half years old (the date is given as 8 May in most manuscripts, 13 May in one), she fell gravely ill. After several days she was believed to be dying, and the last rites were given. A curate set a crucifix before her face and told her to look on it. As she gazed at it, she writes, her pain suddenly left her and she began to see the crucified Christ bleeding, the blood running down from under the crown of thorns, so vividly that it seemed alive. Over that day and the following night she received sixteen 'showings', some seen 'bodily', some as words formed in her understanding, and some as 'spiritual sight'.

Among the best known is the vision of a little thing, the size of a hazelnut, lying in the palm of her hand, round as a ball. She asked what it could be and was answered that it was 'all that is made'; she marvelled that it could last, and understood that it lasts and always will because God loves it. She saw that God made it, loves it and keeps it. She also wrestled with the problem of sin: why, she asked, had God not prevented it? The answer she reports became the most quoted line of her book: "Sin is behovely, but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." (behovely: necessary or fitting)

After the visions she briefly doubted them, telling a visiting priest that she had raved; she was ashamed of the denial, and a final showing confirmed her. She recovered. She wrote down a shorter account (the Short Text), probably soon after, and then, after some twenty years of reflection, a much longer version (the Long Text) with extended theological commentary. There she developed a distinctive theology: God sees in us no wrath; sin is real but cannot finally defeat divine love; and Christ is our mother, who bears us, feeds us with himself and cares for us with a mother's tenderness, an image with roots in Anselm and earlier writers that she made central.

By the early fifteenth century Julian was a respected spiritual counsellor. Margery Kempe, the mystic of King's Lynn, records visiting her around 1413 and receiving advice about discerning her own experiences. Wills mention bequests to Julian between 1393 and 1416, after which she disappears from the record. Her book survived in only a few manuscripts, mainly copied by English Benedictine nuns in exile in France after the Reformation; it was first printed in 1670 by the Benedictine Serenus Cressy.

Julian's book has been read widely since the early twentieth century. Some theologians ask whether her 'all shall be well' implies universal salvation; she herself affirms the Church's teaching about hell while confessing she could not see how her vision fitted with it, leaving the tension unresolved.

keyMoments.text: Julian is born, to judge from her own statement of her age in 1373; her birthplace and original name are unknown.
Aged thirty and a half and believed to be dying, she gazes on a crucifix and begins to receive sixteen 'showings'.
She recovers, briefly doubts the visions, and then writes the Short Text of her Revelations.
Julian is recorded as an anchoress at St Julian's Church, Conisford, Norwich, in a will bequest.
After about twenty years of reflection she completes the Long Text, developing themes such as Christ as mother.
Margery Kempe visits Julian for counsel about her own spiritual experiences.
The last known bequest to Julian is recorded; she probably died soon after.
Serenus Cressy publishes the first printed edition of the Revelations.

experiences.significance: Julian's Revelations is the earliest surviving book in English known to be written by a woman and one of the most influential works of English spirituality. Her optimism about divine love in the face of sin and suffering, her image of Christ as mother and her careful theology of experience have made her popular across Anglican, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers, and she is commemorated on 8 May in Anglican and Lutheran calendars. Theologians debate whether her vision implies universal salvation and how it relates to Augustinian teaching on sin and judgment. She has also become a key figure in feminist theology and in modern contemplative movements, readings that some historians caution can obscure her late medieval context.

experiences.title: Teresa of Ávila: the transverberation and interior castle
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Teresa's Life (Libro de la vida, ch. 29): she sees beside her a small, very beautiful angel holding a long golden spear with a point of fire, which he seems to thrust several times into her heart; drawing it out, he leaves her wholly on fire with love of God, the pain so great it makes her moan yet the sweetness so excessive she does not wish it to stop. She describes the pain as spiritual, though the body shares in it. She also reports raptures and levitations which embarrassed her, and later maps prayer as seven 'mansions' in The Interior Castle (1577).

primarySource.title: Teresa of Ávila, The Book of Her Life; The Interior Castle
primarySource.citation: Libro de la vida 29.13; 20 (raptures); Moradas del castillo interior (1577)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Teresa wrote under obedience to confessors, amid the Spanish Inquisition's suspicion of alumbrados (illuminists) and women visionaries; the Inquisition examined the Life. Several confessors initially told her the visions were demonic. Her reform founded the Discalced Carmelites with John of the Cross.

assessments.text: Canonised 1622 and the first woman Doctor of the Church (1970); her teaching on prayer is a benchmark of orthodox mysticism. The transverberation is commemorated by the Carmelites (26 August) and Bernini's sculpture in Rome.
Her writings are widely read for prayer; many Protestants question raptures and levitations while valuing her realism, humour and Christ-centredness.
Some charismatics draw parallels between her raptures and Spirit-filled experiences; she herself warned that such favours are not the measure of holiness.

Read in the context of the Inquisition, gender and converso ancestry (her grandfather was a Jewish convert); 20th-century psychiatry speculated about hysteria or epilepsy, interpretations now regarded as reductive.

debates: Discernment under the Inquisition: illuminism vs. orthodox mysticism.
Bodily phenomena (levitation) and their value.
experiences.story:
Sixteenth-century Spain was the most powerful Catholic monarchy in Europe, fresh from the conquest of Granada and the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 and building an empire in the Americas. The Spanish Inquisition watched closely for heresy, for Protestant influence and for the alumbrados ('illuminated ones'), mystics accused of claiming direct inspiration that bypassed the Church. Women claiming visions were viewed with particular suspicion. In this setting lived Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada, born in Ávila on 28 March 1515. Her paternal grandfather, a converso (a Christian of Jewish descent) from Toledo, had been penalised by the Inquisition in 1485 for returning to Jewish practice, a fact that came to light only in modern research.

Lively, sociable and fond of romances of chivalry, Teresa entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation in Ávila in 1535, against her father's wishes at first. The convent was large and relatively relaxed: nuns received visitors in the parlour and wealthy sisters kept comfortable apartments. Soon after her profession she fell gravely ill, at one point lying in a coma for days and being taken for dead. For nearly twenty years, by her own account in her Life, she struggled half-heartedly with prayer. A decisive change came around 1554 when, moved by an image of the wounded Christ, she gave herself wholly to prayer, and soon after was deeply affected by reading Augustine's Confessions.

From then on she began to experience intense mystical states, locutions (words heard inwardly) and intellectual visions of Christ. Some confessors feared she was deceived by the devil, and one advised her to make a gesture of contempt at her visions, which she did with great distress. Others, including Jesuit confessors and the Franciscan reformer Peter of Alcántara, reassured her.

In chapter 29 of her Life, written in the early 1560s at her confessors' command, Teresa describes the experience that tradition calls the transverberation (the 'piercing through'). She writes that she saw beside her, on her left side, an angel in bodily form, not large but small and very beautiful, his face so aflame that he seemed one of the highest angels. In his hands she saw a long golden spear with what seemed a point of fire at its tip. He seemed to plunge it several times into her heart, reaching her very entrails, and when he drew it out, she felt he drew them with it and left her wholly on fire with a great love of God. The pain, she wrote, was so great that it made her moan, and yet so surpassing was its sweetness that she could not wish to be rid of it; it was not bodily pain but spiritual, though the body had a share in it. The experience, she says, recurred over some days. It is usually dated around 1559-1560.

Teresa interpreted such experiences as calling her to a stricter, more prayerful life. In 1562, with the support of Peter of Alcántara and the bishop of Ávila but against much local opposition, she founded the small convent of St Joseph in Ávila under the primitive Carmelite rule, with enclosure, poverty and the nuns going barefoot or in sandals ('discalced'). Over the next twenty years she founded seventeen convents for women and, with John of the Cross, whom she met in 1567, began the reform among friars. Her Life was examined by the Inquisition, which held the manuscript for years without condemning it. She wrote The Way of Perfection and, in 1577, The Interior Castle, mapping the soul's journey through seven 'mansions' to union with God.

Teresa died on 4 October 1582 at Alba de Tormes. She was canonised in 1622, alongside Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier. Her heart, preserved at Alba de Tormes, was venerated as bearing a wound; the Carmelites obtained a feast of the Transverberation, kept on 26 August. Gian Lorenzo Bernini sculpted the scene as the Ecstasy of St Teresa (1647-1652) in the Cornaro Chapel of Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome.

Interpretations have varied. Catholic tradition treats the transverberation as a classic instance of a 'wound of love' in mystical theology. Critics, from some Protestant writers to modern psychoanalysts, have read it in erotic or psychological terms, an interpretation encouraged by Bernini's sensual sculpture. Many scholars point out that Teresa herself carefully distinguished spiritual from bodily experience and wrote under pressure to show her orthodoxy to the Inquisition.

keyMoments.text: Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada is born in Ávila to a family of partly converso descent.
She enters the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation in Ávila.
Moved by an image of the wounded Christ, she commits herself wholeheartedly to prayer and begins to experience mystical graces.
According to her Life, an angel pierces her heart with a fiery golden spear, the experience later called the transverberation.
She founds the reformed convent of St Joseph in Ávila, the first house of the Discalced Carmelites.
Teresa meets John of the Cross at Medina del Campo and enlists him for the reform of the friars.
She writes The Interior Castle, her mature account of the soul's journey to union with God.
Teresa dies at Alba de Tormes; she is canonised in 1622 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1970.

experiences.significance: Teresa of Ávila is one of the most influential mystics and reformers of early modern Catholicism: her Discalced Carmelite reform spread worldwide, and her writings on prayer became standard guides to contemplative life. The transverberation became an iconic image of mystical love, especially through Bernini's sculpture, and shaped Baroque spirituality and art. In 1970 she became one of the first two women named Doctors of the Church. Protestant critics historically regarded such visions as unscriptural enthusiasm, and modern readers have offered psychological and erotic interpretations, while scholars emphasise her careful self-scrutiny under the Inquisition's watch and her remarkable achievement as a woman writer in Counter-Reformation Spain.

experiences.title: John of the Cross: the Toledo prison and the 'dark night'
experiences.account: Paraphrase from early biographies and John's own works: seized in December 1577 by Calced Carmelites opposed to Teresa's reform, John is held for about nine months in a tiny cell in Toledo, flogged and underfed. There he composes much of the Spiritual Canticle. He escapes in August 1578. In The Dark Night and The Ascent of Mount Carmel he teaches that the soul is purified by passing through 'nights' of sense and spirit, and warns against attaching importance to visions, locutions and other extraordinary phenomena: the soul should rest in faith alone.

primarySource.title: John of the Cross, The Dark Night; Ascent of Mount Carmel; Spiritual Canticle
primarySource.citation: Ascent of Mount Carmel 2.11 (on rejecting visions); Dark Night 1-2

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: John's teaching was in part a corrective: mystical union is a work of love and faith, not of sensational experiences; this caution became standard Catholic discernment teaching.

assessments.text: Canonised 1726 and Doctor of the Church (1926); 'dark night' theology underpins Catholic spiritual direction.
Orthodox writers find parallels with apophatic theology and the desert fathers' warnings about visions, while noting differences of emphasis.
Read by many evangelicals and Anglicans as a guide to spiritual dryness; some critics fear an overly ascetic, passive spirituality.
'Dark night of the soul' has been compared with depression; spiritual directors and psychologists (e.g. Gerald May) distinguish the two by fruits such as deepened love and freedom.

debates: Visions vs. naked faith: John's critique of extraordinary phenomena.
Spiritual desolation and depression.
experiences.story:
Juan de Yepes was born in 1542 at Fontiveros, a village near Ávila in Old Castile. His father, from a family of wealthy silk merchants, had been disowned for marrying a poor weaver, and died young; his mother Catalina Álvarez raised her sons in poverty, moving to Medina del Campo. There Juan worked in a hospital and studied with the Jesuits. In 1563 he entered the Carmelite order, taking the name Juan de Santo Matía, and studied at the University of Salamanca. Drawn to a more solitary life, he was thinking of joining the Carthusians when, in 1567, newly ordained, he met Teresa of Ávila at Medina del Campo. She persuaded him to help extend her reform to the friars.

In November 1568, at a tiny farmhouse at Duruelo, he and two companions began the first community of Discalced Carmelite friars, and he took the name Juan de la Cruz, John of the Cross. In 1572 Teresa, then prioress of the Incarnation convent in Ávila, brought him there as confessor to the nuns, where he served for five years.

Tensions between the reformed (Discalced) and unreformed (Calced, or 'of the Observance') Carmelites were escalating. The two groups appealed to different authorities: the Calced to the order's general and the papal nuncio, the Discalced to King Philip II and to earlier apostolic visitors. In 1575 a general chapter of the order at Piacenza ordered the Discalced reform to be curtailed. John was regarded by the Calced as a rebel.

On the night of 2-3 December 1577 a group of Calced friars and armed men broke into his lodging at the Incarnation and carried him off. He was taken to the Carmelite priory in Toledo and ordered to renounce the reform; when he refused, he was declared rebellious and imprisoned. His cell, a former closet about six feet by ten, had only a slit high in the wall for light. He was given bread, water and scraps of fish, kept in the same clothes for months and, according to early witnesses, brought regularly before the community in the refectory to be flogged as discipline. He suffered from lice, cold in winter and stifling heat in summer, and was not allowed to celebrate Mass.

In this darkness John composed poetry. Holding the poems in memory and later writing them down with materials obtained from a sympathetic new jailer, he produced most of the Spiritual Canticle, a love poem modelled on the Song of Songs in which the bride searches for her absent beloved; a set of ballads (romances) on the Trinity and Incarnation; and the poem 'For I know well the fount', whose refrain contrasts flowing water with 'although it is night'. The famous poem 'One dark night' (En una noche oscura), describing the soul slipping out of a quiet house by night to meet her Beloved, is often linked to his escape; whether he wrote it in prison or shortly after is debated.

Around the middle of August 1578, after some nine months, John escaped. According to the accounts of his early biographers, he had loosened the screws of the lock and, at night, lowered himself from a window on a rope made of strips of blanket, dropped onto a wall above the Tagus, and found his way through the darkened city to the convent of the Discalced Carmelite nuns, who hid him in their enclosure and then sent him to safety under the protection of a sympathetic canon.

In 1580 Pope Gregory XIII allowed the Discalced to form a separate province, and they later became an independent order. John served as prior and vicar in Andalusia and wrote prose commentaries on his poems: The Ascent of Mount Carmel, The Dark Night, The Spiritual Canticle and The Living Flame of Love. There he developed the teaching that the soul must pass through 'dark nights' of the senses and of the spirit, painful purifications in which consolation and understanding are withdrawn, so that it can be united with God in pure faith and love. In his last years he again fell foul of his own order's leadership and was stripped of office; he died at Úbeda on 14 December 1591. He was canonised in 1726 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1926.

keyMoments.text: Juan de Yepes is born at Fontiveros in Old Castile into a poor family.
Newly ordained, he meets Teresa of Ávila, who recruits him for the reform of the Carmelite friars.
He helps found the first Discalced Carmelite friary at Duruelo and takes the name John of the Cross.
He becomes confessor to the nuns of the Incarnation convent in Ávila.
Calced Carmelites seize him in Ávila and imprison him in a tiny cell in their Toledo priory.
In prison he composes much of the Spiritual Canticle and other poems.
He escapes at night by a rope of blanket strips and takes refuge with the Discalced nuns of Toledo.
The Discalced Carmelites are permitted a separate province, and John later writes his great commentaries including The Dark Night.
John dies at Úbeda; he is canonised in 1726 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1926.

experiences.significance: John of the Cross's imprisonment produced some of the greatest poetry in the Spanish language, and his teaching on the 'dark night of the soul' became a classic framework for understanding spiritual dryness, suffering and purification. His works shaped Catholic mystical theology and have been read widely by Protestants, Anglicans and Orthodox Christians, as well as by philosophers, poets and psychologists. The phrase 'dark night of the soul' has entered everyday language, often loosened from his meaning of a purifying stage toward union with God. Critics have asked whether his stress on detachment from all created things undervalues the world, while admirers see in it a profound account of faith beyond feelings.

experiences.title: Ignatius of Loyola at Manresa and the Spiritual Exercises
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Ignatius' Autobiography (dictated 1553-55, in the third person as 'the pilgrim'): convalescing from a cannonball wound (1521), he reads lives of Christ and the saints and notices the different 'spirits' that leave him consoled or desolate. At Manresa (1522-23) he passes through scruples nearly to despair, then receives illuminations: seeing the Trinity as three keys of a musical instrument, the creation of the world, and, sitting by the river Cardoner, an understanding so great that everything seemed new to him. From these experiences he drafts the Spiritual Exercises, including rules for the discernment of spirits.

primarySource.title: Ignatius of Loyola, Autobiography (Reminiscences); Spiritual Exercises

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: The Inquisition questioned Ignatius in Alcalá and Salamanca on suspicion of being an alumbrado; he was cleared. The Exercises were approved by Pope Paul III in 1548 and became the foundation of Jesuit formation.

assessments.text: The Exercises are among the most influential retreat methods in Catholicism; Ignatian discernment (consolation and desolation) is widely used.
Historically suspicious of the Jesuits, many Protestants now use adapted Ignatian prayer and imaginative reading of the Gospels.

The Autobiography is late and shaped for Jesuit edification, but Ignatius' visionary period and his examination by the Inquisition are documented; John O'Malley stresses the Exercises' practical, pastoral character.
The attention to inner movements has been compared with modern psychology of emotion; T.M. Luhrmann studied related imaginative prayer practices among evangelicals.

debates: Discernment of spirits as a method.
Imagination in prayer: aid or danger?
experiences.story:
Íñigo López de Loyola was born in 1491 in the Basque province of Gipuzkoa, the youngest son of a noble family. Raised for the life of a courtier and soldier, he served in the household of the treasurer of Castile and later the duke of Nájera, viceroy of Navarre. In his own later words, dictated in the third person, he was a man given to the vanities of the world, delighting in the exercise of arms with a great and vain desire to win honour.

On 20 May 1521 French and Navarrese forces besieged Pamplona. Íñigo persuaded the garrison to resist, until a cannonball shattered his right leg. The French, impressed by his courage, carried him home to Loyola. The leg was badly set and had to be rebroken; he nearly died, and later had a protruding bone sawn off out of vanity. During a long convalescence he asked for romances of chivalry, but the only books in the house were a Life of Christ by Ludolph of Saxony and a collection of saints' lives, the Golden Legend. Reading them, he began to imagine imitating Francis and Dominic. He noticed that daydreams of worldly glory left him dry and dissatisfied afterwards, while thoughts of following the saints left him content, an observation he later saw as the beginning of his 'discernment of spirits'. One night, his account says, he saw an image of Our Lady with the child Jesus and felt great consolation.

In early 1522 he left home as a pilgrim. At the Benedictine monastery of Montserrat he made a general confession, gave his fine clothes to a beggar, and on the night of 24-25 March kept a vigil of arms before the image of the Virgin, leaving his sword and dagger at her altar. He then went down to the small town of Manresa, intending to stay a few days. He stayed about eleven months.

At Manresa he lived as a beggar, caring for the sick in a hospital, praying for seven hours a day, fasting severely and letting his hair and nails grow. He often prayed in a cave above the river Cardoner. The first months brought peace, but then came a terrible period of scruples: he repeatedly confessed past sins, never sure he had confessed fully, and at one point was tempted to throw himself from a window. He went a week without food until his confessor ordered him to eat. Finally, he recounts, he decided to stop confessing past sins, and the scruples left him; he concluded that God had freed him.

Then followed what he described as a time when God treated him as a schoolmaster treats a child. He reports experiences of understanding the Trinity as three keys of a musical instrument, of seeing how God created the world, and of Christ's humanity in the Eucharist. The most important came as he sat by the river Cardoner: without seeing any vision, the eyes of his understanding were opened, and he understood many things about spiritual life, faith and learning, with such clarity that, he said, everything seemed new. He later told his secretary that all he had learned in his life together did not equal what he received on that one occasion.

During this period he began to write notes that became the Spiritual Exercises, a four-week programme of meditations, examinations of conscience and rules for discerning spirits, intended to help a person order their life to God. In early 1523 he left for Jerusalem, hoping to stay, but the Franciscan guardians sent him back. He then studied at Barcelona, Alcalá and Salamanca, where he was investigated by church authorities and briefly imprisoned on suspicion of being an alumbrado, and finally at Paris from 1528. There he gathered companions, among them Francis Xavier and Peter Faber, who took vows together at Montmartre on 15 August 1534.

Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus on 27 September 1540, and Ignatius became its first superior general. The Spiritual Exercises were approved in 1548. Our main source for Manresa is the account Ignatius dictated in 1553-1555 to Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, referring to himself as 'the pilgrim'. He died in Rome on 31 July 1556 and was canonised in 1622.

keyMoments.text: Íñigo López de Loyola is born to a noble Basque family at Loyola, Gipuzkoa.
A cannonball shatters his leg during the French siege of Pamplona.
During convalescence at Loyola he reads a Life of Christ and lives of the saints and notices the different 'spirits' that move him.
He keeps a vigil before the Virgin of Montserrat and leaves his sword and dagger at her altar.
At Manresa he lives as a penitent beggar, suffers severe scruples and is tempted to suicide before finding peace.
By the river Cardoner he experiences an 'illumination' of understanding that he later described as the greatest grace of his life.
He leaves Manresa for Jerusalem, carrying early drafts of the Spiritual Exercises.
Pope Paul III approves the Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius and his Paris companions.

experiences.significance: The year at Manresa is the seedbed of the Spiritual Exercises and of the Society of Jesus, which became one of the most influential forces in early modern Catholicism, in education, missions from Japan to Paraguay and the Catholic Reformation. Ignatian discernment of spirits, attentive to inner movements of consolation and desolation, shaped Catholic spirituality and is widely used today by Protestants and others in retreats and spiritual direction. Critics, from Protestant polemicists to Jansenists and Enlightenment writers, attacked the Jesuits for casuistry and political influence, and Ignatius himself was suspected of illuminism in his early years. Historians also note that the main source is his own carefully shaped late recollection.
